Praise is offered to God for the clarity of the proof, and most people, the commentators say, do not grasp this distinction. On "You will die, and they too will die", the exegetes take it as a reminder of mortality and a foretelling of a dispute before God on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that the dispute concerns wrongs between people, and that believers and disbelievers, even the People of the Book, will be involved. Ibn 'Umar relates that the Companions thought the verse concerned them until the strife among them began. As for "most of them", some take it to mean all, others only the people of Mecca or humanity at large.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that he will die, and that those among his people who deny him will die too, after which all will be brought before their Lord on the Day of Resurrection to contend with one another. The plain sense, on which the commentators largely agree, is that death reaches everyone and that the dispute concerns the truthful and the liar, the oppressed and the oppressor, the rightly guided and the misguided. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd, followed by al-Tabari, extend this contention to believers and disbelievers, while Abu al-Aliya understands it as referring to the people of the qibla themselves. Ibn Umar, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri report that some Companions understood the verse as referring to the strife that broke out among them, a reading al-Tabari considers too narrow given the generality of the wording. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite Zubayr's report about injustices being repeated until every person with a right receives it, and Ibn Kathir notes that the verse covers every quarrel of this world. On the difference between mayyit and mayt, al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i hold that the doubled form refers to one who will die and the single form to one whose soul has departed, whereas al-Zamakhshari sees the former as a lasting attribute. The reading with an alif, attributed to Ibn al-Zubayr, is also noted. Al-Razi reads the verse as consoling the Prophet against his opponents, and Ibn al-Qayyim draws lessons on the wisdom of the prophets' deaths. As for the closing lines, the commentators agree that whoever lies against God and calls the truth a lie is destined for Hell, but they differ on who brings the truth and confirms it: Ibn Abbas identifies the Prophet and those who follow him, while Ali and Abu al-Aliya identify Abu Bakr.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ that he will die like every human being, and that those who reject him will die too. Then all of them will be gathered before their Lord on the Day of Resurrection, where He will judge between them. The commentators agree that this dispute on the Day of Judgment is real, but they differ on its scope. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir take it broadly: believers and disbelievers, the wronged against the wrongdoer, the guided against the misguided, the weak against the arrogant. Ibn Zayd specifically understood it as the dispute between Muslims and disbelievers, while Abu al-'Aliya limited it to the people of the qibla among themselves. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also note that the dispute may extend to the soul and the body. Several reports link the verse to the strife among the Companions, as related by Ibn 'Umar, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. Al-Zubayr asked the Prophet ﷺ whether the quarrels of this world would be repeated, and he replied yes, until every right is returned to its owner. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the verse targets the dispute between the disbelievers and the Prophet ﷺ, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi favour the general meaning, supported by the hadith on wrongs between people. Ibn Kathir concludes in favour of the general sense.

This verse states that no one is more unjust than the one who lies about God and denies the truth when it reaches him, and that his abode will be Hell. The commentators explain that lying about God includes attributing a son or a partner to Him, or declaring lawful or forbidden what He has not decreed, while "the truth" is the Qur'an for most of them, the testimony that there is no god but God for Ibn 'Abbas, or the Resurrection and recompense in another reading. The phrase "Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?" is, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur, a rhetorical question affirming this reality.

Opinions differ on "the one who brings the truth and confirms it". Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Abu al-'Aliya take it to be the Prophet, peace be upon him, who brings the truth, and Abu Bakr who confirms it; as-Suddi takes the first to be Gabriel, who brings the Qur'an, and the second to be Muhammad, who receives it; Qatada, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd take it to be the Prophet and the believers who follow him. Others, such as 'Ata' and al-Rabi', take it to mean the prophets and their followers. Al-Tabari prefers to apply it to everyone who calls to the oneness of God, while az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya favour the general sense of believers who speak the truth and believe in it.

Most agree on the conclusion: these are "the God-fearing", and God will give them whatever they wish with their Lord, along with the expiation of their worst deeds. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi also report accounts of the strife among believers mentioned in the surrounding context, but these concern mainly the preceding verse.

This verse describes those who bring the truth and affirm it as the truly God-fearing. The commentators differ on who is meant by "the one who brought the truth". Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, the truth being the testimony that there is no god but God or the Quran, and those who affirmed it being his followers. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya also report the view that the phrase refers collectively to the prophets and their followers, the relative pronoun then carrying a collective sense. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Sa'di adopt this general reading, which covers everyone who calls to the oneness of God.

Other views are recorded. 'Ali, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Kalbi say the one who brought the truth is the Prophet and the one who affirmed it is Abu Bakr. Al-Sudi holds that Gabriel brought the Quran and Muhammad accepted it. Mujahid and others say the believers who bring the Quran on the Day of Resurrection are meant.

There is broad agreement on the overall meaning: the God-fearing are those who avoided polytheism and sins, will receive whatever they wish from their Lord, and will have their worst deeds forgiven and be rewarded for their best. Muqatil, cited by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi, holds that God rewards only their good deeds and does not punish them for bad ones, a view that al-Razi links to the Murji'a. Some readings are also discussed: Abu Salih's reading with a lighter form of the verb is explained as meaning that he deserved the name of truthfulness or acted upon it.

The commentators explain that this verse promises the good-doers that they will have with their Lord whatever their souls desire and their wills seek, as a reward for their righteous conduct in this world. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that ihsan here means perfected piety, whose highest form is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: to worship God as if you see Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya place this bliss in Paradise, while Abu al-Su'ud and Abu Hayyan hold that it also covers the terrors of the Day of Judgment and the period before entering Paradise. Regarding the clause that God will remove from them the worst of what they did, most see it as God covering their gravest sins and recompensing them for their best deeds. Muqatil holds that the reward applies only to good deeds and not to bad ones, a view Razi attributes to the Murji'a. Al-Zamakhshari explains the comparative form by saying that the minor lapses seem grave to them, while their sincere good deeds are most excellent in God's sight; other commentators, including Abu Hayyan, argue that the elative is not meant in its strict sense here. The exegetes generally read the verse as the conclusion of the passage contrasting the liar with the truthful, and as a sign of God's care for those who do good.

This verse says that God will erase from the pious doers the worst of what they did, and will reward them according to their best deeds, which the commentators explain as Paradise and its blessings. There is broad agreement that the promise is for those who brought the truth and affirmed it, and that what they receive is the reward of excellence, as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state.

Scholars differ on who is meant by the one who brought the truth and the one who affirmed it. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd take them to be the Prophet and the believers who followed him, while 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Kalbi name the Prophet and Abu Bakr, and as-Suddi names Gabriel and the Prophet. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari prefer a general reading covering anyone who calls to monotheism, a view al-Shawkani also adopts, whereas az-Zamakhshari restricts it to the Prophet and his companions.

The meaning of "worst" is also debated. Az-Zamakhshari, an-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read the comparative as genuine, referring to the sins the believers regard as gravest, while the two Jalals take the words simply to mean bad and good. Muqatil holds that God rewards only good deeds and not bad ones, a view Ar-Razi reports and criticises and Ibn 'Ashur links to the Murji'a. Ar-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the erasure may cover sins committed before Islam, or major sins committed after faith.

This passage of Surat Az-Zumar affirms that God is sufficient for His servant, meaning the Prophet ﷺ, and answers the pagans who threatened to harm him with madness or misfortune through their idols, which can neither harm nor benefit. The commentators explain that guidance and misguidance belong to God alone: whom He misguides has no guide, and whom He guides has no misleader, a warning to the disbelievers through God's might and vengeance. They agree that the interrogative particle in 'Is not God' affirms the statement, and that 'His servant' refers to the Prophet, as al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd report. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya add that the term may include the Prophet and his followers. The reading differs between the singular, which most readers use, and the plural 'servants', read by Hamza and al-Kisa'i, which Ibn 'Atiyya takes to mean the prophets and believers; Abu 'Ubayd preferred the singular. Ibn Kathir and others report the occasion of revelation: the Quraysh feared their idols would afflict the Prophet, and Qatada tells how Khalid ibn al-Walid smashed the nose of al-'Uzza. Al-Razi sees the verse as consolation for the Prophet and reassurance for his companions. Ibn 'Ashur links it to the parable of the man owned by quarrelling partners. As for the threat, al-Kalbi and as-Suddi understand it as a threat from the idols, al-Razi as human threats, and Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that it covers anyone threatened by what is other than God.

The commentators explain that God alone guides whom He wills, so no one can lead astray those He guides, and whoever He leaves in error has no one to guide him. The rhetorical question "Is not God Mighty, Lord of Retribution?" affirms that God cannot be overcome and that He punishes those who disobey Him and oppose His allies. The exegetes agree that the verse both threatens the idolaters and reassures the believers.

Opinions differ on who "His servant" refers to in "Is not God sufficient for His servant?" Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as the Prophet ﷺ, while the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, "His servants", was taken by al-Mawardi to mean the prophets, and Ibn 'Atiyya took it as a collective noun covering every faithful believer who trusts in God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi explain that God protects His servant from the harm of the idols and the schemes of the idolaters, and al-Jurjani holds that this sufficiency means reward for the believer and punishment for the disbeliever.

All report that the Quraysh threatened the Prophet ﷺ with the vengeance of their idols, some citing the episode in which Khalid ibn al-Walid smashed the idol al-'Uzza. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the question is rhetorical, since God's might is already fixed in human hearts. Ibn Sa'di says that this sufficiency covers matters of religion and of this world, while Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the threat specifically concerns the Prophet ﷺ even though the word "servant" is general. Al-Tabari considers both readings sound and accepts recitation with either.

This verse says that the polytheists acknowledge that God alone created the heavens and the earth. God then tells the Prophet ﷺ to ask them whether the idols they worship besides God could remove a harm that God wills for him, or withhold a mercy that God wills to grant him. The intended answer is no, since these idols have no power at all. The Prophet is then told to say: 'God is sufficient for me,' and that the trusting place their reliance on Him alone. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that the verse is an argument against idolatry, with the question functioning as a rhetorical reproach. Al-Baghawi and al-Sam'ani report that the Prophet asked them and they fell silent, which is why the answer was revealed. On the reading, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr (according to 'Asim) read the words with tanwin and accusative endings, while the others read them in the construct form. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the tanwin, while al-Tabari judged both readings well known and close in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain the feminine forms as referring to al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, or as a sign of their weakness, and Ibn Juzayy notes that these objects are not rational beings. Later scholars such as al-Sha'rawi, Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri restate the same central message: trust in God and rejection of polytheism.

God commands His Messenger to tell his people to act according to their own position, which is one of enmity and disbelief, while he himself acts according to his, which is guidance and monotheism, and that they will soon learn which of the two leads to a good end. The commentators agree on the general sense of the threat. Mujahid explains the word makana as side or direction, Ibn Isa as firm hold, and Yahya as polytheism, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it to mean the state of hostility they have settled into. The phrase 'I too am acting' is left without a complement, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read this omission as intensifying the warning and as signalling that the Prophet's position keeps growing stronger through God's support. As for the humiliation promised, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand it as disgrace in this world and a lasting punishment in the next, whereas Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari connect it with the defeat at Badr in this life and the Fire in the hereafter. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy state that the verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword, but the other commentators do not mention this and do not choose between the views.

This verse, as the commentators explain it, has the Prophet ﷺ address his idolatrous people: act according to your position, and I will act according to mine, and you will soon know who it is that will receive a humiliating punishment and upon whom a lasting punishment will descend. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take the humiliation to be the punishment of this world, which befell the polytheists at Badr, as al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and the authors of the Jalalayn also state. The lasting punishment is, for nearly all commentators, the fire of Hell, though Ibn Kathir places it on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari explains that leaving out the object of "I am acting" intensifies the warning and signals that the Prophet's position keeps growing stronger through God's help. Ibn Ashur notes that the verb "come" suggests a sudden arrival. Al-Mawardi gives three meanings for "makana": the side, the firmness of one's state, or polytheism, while al-Tabari prefers the sense of side. Ibn al-Jawzi reports that some scholars held the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, a view the others do not share. Readings differ between the singular and plural forms of "makana" without changing the core meaning. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin observe that the future tense and the threatening tone are a common way of addressing an obstinate listener.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that He sent down the Book to people with the truth: whoever is guided is guided for his own sake, whoever goes astray harms only himself, and the Prophet is not a guardian over them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read "wakil" as a watcher or guardian, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain "for the people" as meaning for their benefit, so that they are encouraged toward obedience, and they note that God has no need of this; they add that responsibility rests on choice rather than compulsion. Ibn 'Atiyya explains "with the truth" in two ways, either as a Book containing truth in its reports and rulings or as a Book sent down as it was fitting given the good of the world, and he attributes guidance and misguidance to God's creation and the servant's acquisition. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi state that misguidance is confined to the one who chooses it. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Shawkani mention the view that the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword, without deciding. The verse is generally read as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, and the commentators agree that guidance and error depend on personal choice. The following verses, about death and sleep, receive much more varied interpretations, especially on the distinction between the soul and the spirit.

The commentators explain that God takes the souls: He receives them at death, and He also takes those that have not died during sleep. He withholds the soul on which death has been decreed and sends back the other until its appointed term, which is the end of life. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the souls of the living and the dead meet in sleep, and God keeps the souls of the dead and sends back the souls of the sleepers to their bodies. Al-Tabari also cites the view that sleep is a lesser death in which the soul is held back from action. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the verb as a figure, since the sleeper, like the dead, does not discern or act, and they hold that the soul taken in both states is one. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy draw the lesson that guidance and misguidance come only from God, just as life, waking, death and sleep do. Ibn Abbas distinguishes two elements, the soul of discernment that withdraws in sleep and the breath-spirit that remains; Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan mention that others regard soul and spirit as one, yet most, including Ibn Kathir, consider this question too subtle to settle with certainty. The broad conclusion shared by most is that the verse shows God's power and His ability to raise the dead. On recitation, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb in the passive, while the majority read it in the active.

In this verse God rebukes the polytheists who take idols besides Him as intercessors they believe will bring them near to Him, and commands the Prophet ﷺ to ask them how they can take as intercessors beings that own nothing and have no reason. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the intercessors to be the idols, and the question as a rebuke. The commentators agree that all intercession belongs to God alone, that no one can intercede with Him except by His permission, that He owns the heavens and the earth, and that all return to Him. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that intercession benefits only when God permits the intercessor and is pleased with the one interceded for, and that the polytheist is not approved. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes the rejected intercession of a rival partner from the accepted intercession of a permitted servant. Al-Razi links the verse to consoling the Prophet over his people's stubbornness, and notes that guidance and misguidance are in God's hands. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that 'am' here is disjunctive, meaning 'rather' with a question, and that the following verse on hearts recoiling describes the polytheists' aversion to monotheism. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi mention the story of the 'Gharaniq' reported by some, which other commentators reject. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the question aims to refute the polytheists' excuses.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say that all intercession belongs to Allah alone. He is its owner, and no one can intercede with Him except by His permission and for someone He approves of. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Him you will be returned. The commentators explain that the pagans took idols as intercessors with God, and the Quran answers that these idols own nothing and have no reason. There is broad agreement that intercession happens only with God's permission, and that the verse refutes the pagans' claim about their deities. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir stress that no one intercedes without His leave, and that all intercession returns to Him. Al-Zamakhshari holds that intercession is accepted only when two conditions are met: the one interceded for must be approved and the intercessor must be authorised. Al-Razi says that all intercession belongs to God, and that the verse cannot be used to deny intercession altogether, a view also taken by al-Alusi. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes the rejected intercession of a partner from the intercession of a servant who intercedes only after his Lord has authorised him. Ibn 'Ashur explains the rhetorical question and the adverbial use of 'jami'an'. On the particle 'am', Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Uthaymin treat it as disjunctive, meaning 'bal' with a question. Commentators differ on the identity of these idols: some take them to be images of righteous people, others angels. The account of the 'gharaniq' episode, which several exegetes mention, is not part of the direct meaning of this verse.

This verse describes the state of those who do not believe in the Hereafter: when God is mentioned alone, their hearts recoil and shrink, yet when their deities are mentioned instead, they rejoice. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the verb ishma'azza means to recoil, shrink or be repelled from monotheism, while Qatada, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as arrogance or disdain. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi cite the sense of contraction or aversion, and al-Qurtubi also gives the sense of rejection. All agree that istibshar means joy that shows on the face, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the two reactions are opposite extremes. Several commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya, connect the verse to the episode of the gharaniq, when Satan cast words into the Prophet's recitation of Surat al-Najm before the Kaaba; Ibn Ashur considers this link distant from the verse's context. Al-Razi argues that rejoicing at idols shows deep ignorance, since mentioning God is the source of all good, while idols are lifeless and foolish. Ibn Sa'di adds that this state is among the worst, and that the matter will be judged on the Day of Recompense.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to turn to Him in supplication, saying: O God, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You alone judge between Your servants concerning what they differed about. The commentators explain that this disagreement concerns religion, the oneness of God and faith in Him, and some take it to mean disagreement about guidance and error. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the verse comes in the context of the polytheists recoiling when God alone is mentioned and rejoicing when their idols are named, so the Prophet is told to leave their fate to God. The scholars agree that the verse consoles the Prophet, teaches believers to call upon God by His names, and warns the obstinate. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that this supplication was part of the Prophet's night prayer, citing the hadith of Aisha. For the verses that follow, the exegetes agree that the disbelievers, even if they owned everything on earth and as much again, could not ransom themselves from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, that what appears to them from God will exceed what they expected, and that the evil deeds they earned will surround them. Mujahid and al-Suddi say they took their deeds to be good when they were evil, while others say they did not believe in resurrection. The commentators do not choose between these readings and regard them all as possible.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection: even if they possessed everything on earth and as much again, they would offer it to ransom themselves from the terrible punishment, yet it would not be accepted, and what they had not reckoned with from God would appear to them. Most exegetes, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that the address concerns disbelievers and associators, and that the verse magnifies the severity of the punishment and removes all hope of ransom. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report that what appears may be God's wrath they had not expected, or deeds they thought were good that turn out to be evil, a view attributed to al-Suddi and Mujahid. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi also cite Sufyan al-Thawri's warning against ostentation drawn from this verse. Al-Razi holds instead that it refers to kinds of punishment beyond their reckoning, much as the delights of Paradise are beyond imagination. Al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him read it as an amplification of the threat. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that some considered it applicable to Muslims too, and al-Hasan saw in it a warning against usury. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the verb badā means that what appears exceeds whatever they had imagined.

This verse describes how, on the Day of Judgement, the disbelievers will see the evil consequences of what they earned in this world, and the punishment they used to mock will surround them. The commentators explain that what becomes apparent is the outcome of their deeds, and that this recompense is called 'evil deeds' because it matches their wrongdoing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi understand these as the sinful deeds committed in worldly life, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan add that the records of their deeds will be displayed to them, though they had forgotten them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi note that 'evil deeds' may also mean the punishments themselves, citing the verse 'the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it.' Ibn Kathir reports Sufyan al-Thawri's warning to the hypocrites and the distress of Ibn al-Munkadir at his death. On the verb 'kasaba', Ibn Abbas and others understand it as deliberate acquisition, and al-Sha'rawi explains that the Qur'an uses 'kasaba' for wrongdoing because it can become habitual and second nature. Ibn 'Uthaymin draws from this that humans acquire their own deeds, against those who hold that they are compelled. There is broad agreement that the punishment falls on those who mocked the Prophet's warnings. Ibn 'Ashur observes that 'ma' may be relative or verbal and that 'what they used to mock' refers to the punishment itself. No commentator gives a specific occasion of revelation for this verse.

The verse describes a human reaction: when harm touches a person, he calls upon God; but when God grants him a blessing, he claims it was given to him because of knowledge he possesses. God replies that this blessing is a trial, though most people do not realise it. The commentators agree that 'man' here refers to humankind in general, and that the blessing is a test rather than a sign of divine approval. Al-Tabari explains 'on knowledge' as meaning that God knows the recipient deserves it, or as a good thing with God; Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report similar views. Ibn 'Atiyya distinguishes two readings: if the knowledge is the person's own knowledge of ways to gain, it is self-admiration; if it is God's knowledge, it is presumption and a claim upon God. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the connective 'fa' sets this verse apart from the 'waw' at the start of the surah, because it follows from the aversion shown to the remembrance of God. Ibn Kathir sees the passage as a warning against pride, while Ibn al-Qayyim argues that wealth is no proof of divine favour, citing the story of Qarun. Muqatil, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, identifies Qarun as the speaker of these words. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that blessings can be a means of gradual deception. Al-Sa'di, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi stress that the expansion and restriction of provision follow divine wisdom and not God's love or anger toward the individual.

The commentators explain that the verse reports the words of the person who calls upon God in hardship but, once given a blessing, claims he has it through his own knowledge or merit; God answers that it is a test. Earlier peoples, among them Qarun, said the same, and their gains did not save them from punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi focus mainly on Qarun and the past nations, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also allow that it refers to entire nations, or to Qarun and his people who approved his words. Most agree that the unjust among the Quraysh will meet a similar fate, and the commentators cite the famine followed by rain after seven years and the defeat at Badr. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan lay out the possible meanings of 'on knowledge': knowledge of God regarding the person's merit, or the person's own knowledge of how to earn. Ibn al-Qayyim stresses that a blessing should be credited to God's grace rather than to oneself. According to Ibn Sa'di and al-Razi, the widening and narrowing of provision follow divine wisdom and are not a sign of God's love or anger, and only believers benefit from these signs.

This passage from Surah Az-Zumar describes the fate of those who attribute God's blessings to their own knowledge and earnings rather than to His grace. The commentators explain that earlier peoples, such as Qarun, said the same thing, yet the wealth they gained did not benefit them, and they were struck in this life by the consequences of their misdeeds.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di note that the verse warns the disbelievers of Mecca that the same will befall them. Al-Tabari and al-Nasafi say this was fulfilled through seven years of drought and the killing of their leaders at Badr. Abu al-Su'ud and Abu Hayyan, however, allow that the punishment meant may be the one in the afterlife or something broader, while al-Alusi prefers the worldly punishment as better suited to the context.

Most exegetes agree that God's bounties are a test and not a sign of approval. Al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that wealth and health may be a gradual trial. Ibn Kathir adds that the proud person thinks he deserves these gifts. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya offer several readings of the phrase "by knowledge I have been given": some take it as knowledge of ways to earn, others as God's knowledge of the speaker's worth. Ibn 'Atiyya judges the first reading to contain self-admiration and the second to contain presumption before God.

All agree that God extends and restricts provision according to His wisdom, and that faith is what allows one to perceive these signs. The duty to turn back to God and follow the best of what was revealed is stressed by Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Sa'di as a practical application, and the commentators agree that the Qur'an is the best of what was sent down.

This verse describes a person who calls upon God in distress, but once the hardship is lifted and a blessing is given, claims it came to him because of knowledge he has of his own worth. The commentators answer that the blessing is a trial, not a proof of merit, and that most people do not realize this. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the verse refutes the notion that wealth shows God's favour, since God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it to whom He wills. They differ on the meaning of 'upon knowledge': Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it as a good standing God knows in him, al-Hasan as knowledge God taught him, Mujahid as a higher rank, and Qatada elsewhere as knowledge of ways to gain wealth. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi report that these words were the claim of Qarun and those who approved of him. Ibn al-Qayyim holds that the text blames whoever attributes a blessing to his own knowledge or merit instead of to God's grace. Al-Razi points to the contradiction of one who calls on God in hardship yet credits his own effort for good fortune. Most read 'yaqdir' as restricting provision, and take 'signs for a people who believe' to mean signs for those who reflect and benefit from them. Al-Tabari links the verse to the preceding discussion of the polytheists, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a rebuke to those who fail to recognise that provision lies in God's hand.

The commentators agree that this verse carries a message of hope to everyone who has transgressed against himself through sin: they must not despair of God's mercy, for God forgives all sins to those who repent, and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that forgiveness is tied to repentance, and that associating partners with God cannot be forgiven without it, citing the verse in al-Nisa' that God does not forgive association but forgives what is less than that to whom He wills. Al-Mawardi gives three senses of forgiveness: by repentance, by pardon except for association, or by forgiving minor sins for those who avoid major ones. Al-Razi argues that the wording suggests a general forgiveness, while still requiring repentance, and notes that forgiveness may come immediately or after punishment. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya record the same debate.

On the occasion of revelation, opinions differ. Some report it concerned Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza; others 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a and al-Walid ibn al-Walid and their companions who had apostatised under torture; others the Meccans who thought their crimes unforgivable. Al-Tabari notes that the most famous report is that of 'Umar, who wrote the verse out by his own hand. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi nonetheless observe that the verse's scope goes beyond the particular cause. Commentators also cite 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar as calling it the most hopeful verse of the Quran.

The following verses call for turning back to God and submitting to Him before punishment comes, for following the best of what was revealed, and warn against the soul saying: alas, for my neglect of God's side. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy read this as regret for not obeying. The final verse rejects the wish, 'if God had guided me I would have been among the righteous', answering that the signs came and were denied out of arrogance.

This verse calls people, including those who have wronged themselves through sin, to turn back to their Lord in repentance, obedience and sincere submission before a punishment comes upon them from which no one can be rescued. The commentators link this call to the preceding verses that announce forgiveness, and show that repentance is the means of obtaining it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain inaba as returning to obedience and giving up disbelief and sin. Al-Zamakhshari holds that mentioning repentance right after the promise of forgiveness keeps anyone from hoping for it without repenting, while al-Razi argues that repentance is always required, and that forgiveness may come at once or only after some punishment. On the phrase "follow the best of what was sent down to you", al-Hasan takes it to mean committing to obedience and avoiding disobedience, al-Suddi means what God commanded in the Book, and Ibn Zayd means the clear verses. Regarding "lest a soul say: Alas", most explain it as the regret, on the Day of Judgment, of one who neglected obedience to God or who mocked the religion. Al-Alusi and al-Qurtubi note that the "law" in "if only I had a return" expresses a wish rather than a condition. All agree the verse urges haste toward repentance, but they differ on the precise meaning of inaba and ihsan.

In this verse God urges His servants to follow the best of what was sent down to them from their Lord before punishment comes upon them suddenly while they are unaware. The commentators differ over what this "best" means. Al-Hasan, as-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the whole Qur'an is good, and that the point is to obey God by doing what He commands and avoiding what He forbids, relying on its clear verses. Al-Tabari holds that it means following its commands, prohibitions, reports and parables, the best of which is to comply with its orders and refrain from its prohibitions, since the prohibition is itself part of what was revealed. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the best refers to the Qur'an, or to the abrogating rather than the abrogated text. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the comparative form expresses the perfection of goodness rather than a ranking among verses, and that the address is to the polytheists who are told to follow. As for the punishment, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari take it to be punishment in this world, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi include punishment in the hereafter. All agree that suddenness means the person does not perceive the punishment before it strikes, which makes it harder to bear.

This verse calls those who have wronged themselves through excess to turn back to God and submit to Him before the punishment comes, and warns them of the day when a soul will cry out in regret: "Oh, my grief over what I neglected regarding God, and I was among the mockers!" The commentators explain that "yā ḥasratā" is an exclamation of regret, with the alif replacing the first-person ya, and that it is read in several ways. Most agree that "fī janb Allāh" means neglecting obedience to God and His right, while al-Farrā' and Ibn al-A'rābī take janb to mean nearness, so the sense becomes neglecting the pursuit of Paradise. Al-Zamakhsharī sees the phrase as a metonymy. Qatāda explains the mockery: the one who neglected obedience did not stop there but went on to ridicule those who obey. Reports link the verse to pagans who had committed murder and adultery and asked about repentance, and some say it concerns Wahshī, slayer of Hamza, though Ibn 'Abbās and others hold it general. On "had God guided me," opinions differ: al-Zamakhsharī and the Mu'tazilites read it as the revelation already received and rejected, while Ibn Kathīr and al-Jazā'irī take it as an empty wish refuted by God's reply, "Indeed, My signs came to you," and Ibn Kathīr notes that even if they were returned they would revert to what they were forbidden.

This part of verse 39:57 records the wish of a negligent soul on the Day of Judgment: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the righteous." Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir place it within a sequence of speeches attributed to different souls: first regret, "Alas, for what I neglected regarding Allah", then the excuse of not having been guided, and finally the wish to return to the world to do good. The commentators agree that these are the words of someone who repents too late and clutches at an excuse that will not help.

Scholars differ on what "guided" means. Al-Zamakhshari, writing from a Mu'tazili position, distinguishes guidance by compulsion, which he rejects as contrary to wisdom, guidance by grace, which this person did not merit, and revelation, which had reached them but was ignored. Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud understand guidance as direction and showing the way to the truth. Al-Nasafi takes it as divine help and protection, and holds that the disbeliever knows God's guidance better than the Mu'tazilites do. Abu Hayyan relates it to God creating the act of being guided.

Ibn 'Ashur sees "law" here as an expression of wish or justification, explaining that the soul repeats the excuses it used to offer in the world. Ibn Kathir notes that the Qur'an states that even if they were returned to earth, they would not be guided.

This verse describes the regret of souls on the Day of Judgment: they lament having neglected their duty toward God, meaning obedience to Him, and admit they used to mock those who served Him. The commentators explain that "soul" here refers to the soul of the disbeliever or the wrongdoer, and that the indefinite form signifies a multitude or a category of souls. Opinions differ on the meaning of "janb" (side or right): al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as obedience or God's command; Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak as the remembrance of God and the Quran; al-Farra' and Ibn 'Arafa as nearness, that is, Paradise; al-Zamakhshari sees it as a metaphor for God's right and standing. As for the phrase "if God had guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing", al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read it as an excuse based on predestination, and al-Zamakhshari replies that God had already guided the soul through revelation, which it did not follow. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that after a return to the world they would not be guided. Ibn 'Ashur regards these claims as futile excuses and takes the "law" in "if only I had a return" as expressing a wish. The "doers of good" are understood by Ibn Kathir as those who obey sincerely, by al-Nasafi as monotheists, and by Ibn Juzayy and al-Jalalayn as believers. The verse ends with God's answer: yes, My signs came to you, but you denied them and grew arrogant, which rejects their wish.

This verse records the words of a soul which, on the Day of Resurrection, laments having neglected its duty toward God, pleads that no guidance reached it, or wishes to return to the world to be among the good-doers. God's reply is: 'Yes indeed, My signs came to you, but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers.' The commentators explain the regret as neglect of obedience, and 'side of God' as His right, His command, or His obedience. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya stress that the reply places responsibility on the soul itself, while al-Razi lays out the theological arguments about human capacity and discusses them without settling the matter. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read the particle 'bala' as a rejection of the claimed excuse of lacking guidance, since revelation had indeed come. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that 'bala' answers an implied negation. The readings differ: most read the verb in the masculine, while a feminine reading attributed to 'A'isha and Umm Salama is recorded. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, mention a occasion of revelation concerning idolaters who had committed murder and adultery and asked whether they could repent; these reports link the subsequent verses on forgiveness to that event. Opinions differ on how far that occasion limits the general application of the verses, with many extending the promise of forgiveness to all who repent.

On the Day of Resurrection, the verse says, the Prophet will see those who lied about God, attributing to Him a partner or a son or declaring things lawful and unlawful on their own authority, and their faces will be blackened, a sign of the distress and disgrace that overtake them. God then affirms that Hell is the abode of the proud who refuse faith and obedience. The commentators agree that blackened faces mark the people of the Fire, and that lying about God means any attribution to Him that does not befit Him. Al-Zamakhshari, in a polemical passage, lists views he attributes to the Qadariyya and the Mu'tazila; al-Qadi, as reported by al-Razi, holds that the verse covers anyone who describes God in ways that do not befit Him, whether by denial or affirmation. Al-Razi rejects limiting the verse to Jews and Christians or to the Arab polytheists, and he restricts the lie to a deliberate one, excluding the mujtahid who errs in good faith.

Opinions differ on the nature of the blackness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as a real discoloration or a visible sign, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi allow that it may express grief, affliction and despair, and al-Razi sees a spiritual darkness born of ignorance of God. On pride, Ibn 'Atiyya defines it as raising oneself above one's right, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that its gravest degree is polytheism.

The verse then turns to the fate of the righteous: God saves them through their mafaza, meaning their triumph or their deliverance, and they neither suffer harm nor grieve. Al-Mawardi gives several readings: deliverance from the Fire, the success that comes from obedience, or the reward of a hard journey. A plural reading, mafazat, is attested among some reciters, and al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad consider both forms acceptable.

God delivers those who were mindful of Him, by their attainment, from the fire of Hell. They will not be touched by evil, nor will they grieve. The commentators differ on the meaning of mafaza, the word for their salvation or success. Al-Tabari, quoting al-Suddi, takes it to mean their virtues, while Ibn Zayd and, according to al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, Ibn Abbas understood it as their good deeds. Al-Mawardi, al-Mubarrad and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean the success itself, namely deliverance from the Fire and entry into Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari also notes that the clause about not being touched by evil may explain what that success is. On the reading, most read the singular, whereas Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read the plural, which some explain by the variety of ways of being saved. Al-Razi links the promise to the preceding warning about those who lied against God and whose faces turn black, and notes that believers will not be overcome by the great terror. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that the negation of harm and sorrow is lasting, covering both what is past and what is to come.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God alone creates everything and that He watches over everything, arranging it according to His will. Everything lies under His management, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain, giving 'wakil' the sense of guardian and one who bears responsibility for the matter.

The exegetes agree that the verse rejects the idea that any other power creates or governs. They differ on the meaning of 'wakil': some see a guardian, others one who guarantees the completion of a matter, and Ibn 'Ashur stresses its role as evidence for tawhid. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya connect the verse to its context, al-Zamakhshari treating it as a parenthesis between two passages, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi read the structure differently.

The commentators also explained the word 'maqalid'. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid took it to mean keys, al-Sudi treasuries, Qatada keys of provision and mercy, and al-Kalbi treasuries of rain and plants. Several cite a hadith on its meaning attributed to 'Uthman, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy note the weakness of its chain.

The Mu'tazilites used this verse to argue that the Quran is created. Ibn al-Qayyim records the response of the people of tradition, for whom God's attributes are part of His name and the Creator is not created. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that a general statement may be restricted. Al-Sha'rawi, finally, distinguishes the act created by God from the orientation of the will by the human being.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God alone holds the keys of the heavens and the earth, meaning the control of their treasures and the management of their affairs, giving to whom He wills and withholding from whom He wills. Most agree that the maqalid are keys: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid note that the word is Persian for keys, while al-Suddi and al-Tabari take it to mean treasures. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Muqatil explain them as rain, provision and vegetation, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read them as a metaphor for sovereignty and protection. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir cite the report from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan that the keys are the formulas of tawhid and glorification, but Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya regard that report as weak or strange. On the second part of the verse there is broad agreement: those who deny God's signs are the losers, having lost reward and salvation, and al-Tabari links this loss to being deprived of the blessings of the heavens in the Hereafter and of divine help in this world. The scholars differ on how the verse connects to its context: al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan attach it to the verse about God saving the righteous, while al-Razi attaches it to what immediately precedes. The overall meaning remains an affirmation of divine power together with a warning against rejecting God's signs.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to answer the polytheists who asked him to worship their idols alongside God: how could he obey a command to worship other than the One who holds the keys of the heavens and the earth? The commentators agree that calling them 'ignorant' refers to their ignorance of God's greatness and power. Several reports cited from Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and others say that the Quraysh proposed that he touch some of their idols while they would believe in his God, or that they would worship his God for a year and he would worship their idols for a year. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand 'maqalid' as keys or treasuries; Ibn 'Atiyya adds that this may be a figurative expression, and Ibn 'Ashur links it to God's full dominion. Grammatically, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud explain that 'ghayr' is governed by 'a'budu' or by 'ta'murunni', with 'an' understood; the readers differ on how the nun of 'ta'murunni' is written. The overall meaning given is that worship is due only to the One who holds all sovereignty, and that association is an ignorance.

This verse states that God revealed to the Prophet ﷺ and to the messengers before him that if they associated partners with God, their deeds would be void and they would be among the losers. The commentators read it mainly as a warning against shirk and an affirmation of its gravity. Al-Tabari treats the verse as an inversion of word order, meaning that if one associates, one's deeds will be nullified and one will perish. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi point out that the prophets are protected from shirk, so the condition is hypothetical; impossible things may be supposed for a purpose, namely to stir the addressee, to discourage the unbelievers and to show how monstrous association is. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi observe that although the Prophet is addressed, the real audience is his community, and Ibn Kathir reports that the verse answers pagans who asked the Prophet to worship their gods. On how far the nullification reaches, the Hanafis, as reported by Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, hold that apostasy voids all earlier deeds, while al-Shafi'i, as cited by al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, limits it to dying in disbelief, relying on the verse of al-Baqara. Ibn 'Ashur sees a comparison with a merchant who loses his capital. The verse is framed by the preceding statement that God is the creator of all things and the following command to worship God alone and be grateful.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to answer those who invited him to worship their idols: he is to devote worship to God alone and to be among those who give thanks for His favours. The commentators agree that the verse affirms exclusive worship of God and rejects associationism. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Sa'di note that placing the object 'Allah' before the verb signifies restriction and exclusivity. They differ on the role of the particle 'fa': al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari take it as the answer to an implied condition, al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i as marking an implied verb before it, and al-Akhfash as a superfluous particle. Many understand gratitude as doing good deeds; al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi specify gratitude for guidance and note that the Prophet was made the master of the sons of Adam. Nearby verses say that associating partners with God voids one's deeds. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di hold that the address is to the Prophet while the intended audience is others, since God preserved him from shirk, whereas al-Qurtubi reports that the voiding is conditional on dying in disbelief. For the following verse about the earth held in His grip and the heavens folded in His right hand on the Day of Resurrection, most exegetes cite Ibn 'Abbas, who says everything is in His right hand, while others place the heavens in the right hand and the earth in the left; some understand the hand as power and dominion. Al-Tabari reports that the verse was revealed in response to a Jew asking about God's attributes, while Ibn 'Ashur regards this occasion as disputed.

The verse says that the idolaters did not measure God with the measure He deserves when they associated partners with Him. It then depicts His immense power: on the Day of Resurrection the whole earth will be in His grip and the heavens folded in His right hand, and He is exalted above what they associate with Him. Commentators differ on the meaning of not measuring God truly. Al-Tabari reports that it refers to the unbelievers who did not accept God's power over them, and Ibn Kathir and al-Suddi take it as worshipping idols and inviting the Prophet to do so, while Mujahid links it to the Quraysh, and al-Mawardi lists three meanings, one of them being false description of God. On the grip and the right hand, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir keep the wording as it stands, affirming it without asking how, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi read them as images of power and dominion without literal motion. Al-Sa'di and the Muyassar stress God's greatness, and Ibn Ashur sees the image as showing absolute sovereignty. Several works cite the hadith of the Jewish rabbi who said God holds the heavens on one finger, at which the Prophet laughed, and they differ on how to read it. On the trumpet, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi describe two blasts, the first causing all to swoon and the second raising them up. They differ on who is excepted: Ibn Abbas names Gabriel, Michael, Israfil and the Angel of Death, while Abu Hurayra names the martyrs.

The verse describes the blowing of the Trumpet: it is blown, and everyone in the heavens and on earth falls senseless (dead or stunned), except those God wills; then it is blown again, and behold, they stand up, looking on. The commentators agree that the first blast is the blast of the swoon and the second the blast of resurrection, and that Israfil is the one who blows it. On the exception, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, citing al-Suddi and a hadith from Anas, names Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and the Angel of Death, who will die afterwards; Ibn Kathir repeats this account. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and a hadith from Abu Hurayra identify the martyrs, standing around the Throne with swords at their sides; al-Hasan takes it to mean God alone. Others mention the houris and youths of Paradise, the guardians of Paradise and Hell, or the bearers of the Throne. Al-Tabari judges the Abu Hurayra hadith the sounder report, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the swooning may be a loss of consciousness rather than death. The exegetes also report that the interval between the two blasts is forty, though whether days, months or years is unknown. Some mention Moses, whose hadith says he may have been spared or may have swooned and then revived, and opinions vary on this. A few count three blasts rather than two.

This verse depicts the Day of Judgment, when the earth shines with the light of its Lord, the Book is placed for reckoning, the prophets are brought forward to be asked whether they delivered the message and what their peoples answered, and the witnesses are present. God then judges between people with justice, and no one is wronged, neither by a reduction of good deeds nor an increase of bad ones.

The commentators broadly agree that the Book refers to the records of deeds, though Qatada, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir state this explicitly, while al-Sudi takes it to mean the reckoning itself, and some mention the Preserved Tablet. They also agree that judging with truth means judging with justice.

Opinions differ on the light of the earth. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and al-Sudi read it as God's justice, whereas Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi understand a created light that illuminates the plain of gathering. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari accept the figurative reading of justice as light while allowing the literal one, and al-Alusi leaves the matter open, noting the manifestation of God's presence.

The witnesses are also debated. Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari and most scholars identify them with the community of Muhammad, who will testify that the prophets delivered the message. Ata, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd take them to be the recording angels, while Qatada and al-Sudi understand them as those who died as martyrs in God's cause. Al-Tabari prefers the first view because it fits the context of the prophets and their peoples.

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection every soul will be paid in full for what it did, whether good or evil, and that God, who knows best what people do, is fully aware of their obedience and disobedience in this world. The commentators agree that this recompense is complete, with nothing reduced and nothing added. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that God needs neither a scribe nor a witness to know what was done, though the Book of Deeds and the witnesses are brought forward to establish the proof. Ibn Kathir supports this with verses about the scales and justice. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the verb wuffiyat signifies a complete payment, and they find in the verse a warning to the disbelievers. Al-Alusi, al-Shawkani and Ibn Sa'di connect the verse to the scene of the Last Day that precedes it, with the trumpet blast, the earth shining with God's light, the placing of the Book, and the coming of the prophets and witnesses, and Ibn Sa'di holds that the judgment there is perfectly just. Al-Biqa'i remarks that speaking of deeds and of knowledge suits the context of recompense. Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari note that the verse describes recompense matching the deed exactly. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that full recompense is realized only on the Last Day, whereas in this world it is not always complete for non-believers.

This verse describes the disbelievers being driven into Hell in successive groups. When they arrive, its gates are opened and its keepers rebuke them with a question that leaves them no excuse: did messengers from among themselves not come to recite to them the signs of their Lord and warn them of the meeting with this day? They admit that the messengers came, but the word of punishment has been fulfilled against the disbelievers. The commentators agree on the general sense: they are driven violently and humiliatingly toward punishment, after the proof has been established. On the word zumar, al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi understand distinct groups following one another, while al-Kalbi takes them to be nations, and Ibn Kathir and al-Razi stress the harshness of the driving. On the particle wa before "futihat", the Kufans and others regard it as superfluous, while others read it as a circumstantial wa; al-Zajjaj, Ibn Juzayy and al-Sa'di hold that the answer to "idha" is omitted. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that the sudden opening of the gates intensifies the suffering. Ibn Kathir identifies the word of punishment with the divine statement "I will fill Hell". Al-Razi draws from the passage that responsibility does not arise before revelation, a point Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss without settling. The commentators do not decide between these views; the text is read for what it says.

This verse describes the fate of the disbelievers as they enter Hell. After they admit that the messengers had come and the proof was established against them, they are told: enter the gates of Hell, to remain in it forever; how evil is the abode of the arrogant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi agree that those who speak are the keepers of Hell or the angels, that eternity is decreed in advance rather than already realised, that the abode is Hell, and that arrogant refusal to accept the truth is what brought them there. Al-Razi and al-Biqa'i link the punishment both to arrogance and to the word of punishment already decreed, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that the gates of Hell are described without the particle that marks the opening of the gates of Paradise. Al-Razi draws from this that no one is held accountable before the prophets came. The commentators stress that the command to enter is a humiliation rather than an honour. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the questions put to the damned are rebukes, and that the word gates refers to successive entrances. On the wa particle and the grammatical structure of the conditional sentence, the grammarians differ, as discussed by al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan. The commentators agree on the general meaning of the verse; the differences concern mainly the precise cause of entry and the grammar.

This verse describes the God-fearing being led into Paradise in groups, a procession of honour rather than humiliation like that of the disbelievers. The commentators explain that "sīqa" conveys urgency: Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi speak of riding mounts, while al-Razi also sees it as the heart's longing for the meeting with God. On arrival they find the gates already open, and the keepers greet them with peace and say "Tayyibtum", that is, you are purified, so enter to dwell forever.

The scholars agree that entry into Paradise is linked to purity. Mujahid takes this as obedience to God, Ibn Abbas as the pleasantness of the abode, al-Dahhak as blessing, and al-Farra' as purification. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim stress the purity of deeds and of the soul, while the Mu'tazila draw from it the view that no sinner enters without repentance, a point al-Razi discusses.

The main disagreement concerns the answer to the conditional "hatta idha". Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj hold it to be omitted, al-Akhfash and the Kufans take the waw as superfluous, and al-Zamakhshari and others read it as a waw of circumstance. Ibn Kathir also reports the tradition that the believers wait at the gate until the Prophet intercedes for its opening.

The inheritors of the earth are, according to Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, the land of Paradise, while another view refers it to the earth of this world. They then say: "Praise be to God who has fulfilled His promise to us." The passage closes with the angels encircling the Throne glorifying their Lord, and with the words "Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds", which several commentators take as the closing of every matter.

This verse describes what the people of Paradise say once they have entered it: they praise God who fulfilled His promise to them and gave them the land of Paradise, where they settle wherever they wish, and they declare that the reward of those who acted well is excellent. The commentators agree that "inheritance" here is a figure of speech meaning possession and the freedom to dispose of something, and that "the land" is the land of Paradise. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi hold this view, and Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi support it with similar verses. Al-Mawardi reports two opinions, that it means the land of Paradise or the land of this world, without choosing between them. Al-Tabari explains "settling" as taking up residence and dwelling, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that each person has a vast garden and needs no other's. Several authors, including al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi, link the praise to thanks for the fulfilment of the promise. For the reward, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it to be the Garden given to the obedient. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also relate reports about the first to enter and about the gates of Paradise, but these reports are not part of the verse's own wording.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection after both groups have been settled: the angels are seen surrounding the Throne, glorifying their Lord with His praise, judgment is passed with justice, and then it is said: Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The commentators agree that the Throne means a seat or place of sovereignty, and that the angels encircle it on every side. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Suddi explain the surrounding as encompassing, while al-Razi notes that the angels praise God for the justice of His judgment. On the nature of the glorification, al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi call it a pleasure rather than worship, since religious obligation has ceased that day, whereas Ibn Uthaymin holds that it is also worship and that obligation continues on that day. Regarding the phrase "with the praise of their Lord", al-Hasan is cited by al-Mawardi as meaning knowledge of God, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi connect it to glorification through praise. As for the judgment between creatures, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan extend it to all servants or, in another reading, to the angels according to their ranks, while Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn take it as a judgment between believers and disbelievers. Finally, the identity of the one who says the closing praise remains open: Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir leave it general, al-Baghawi attributes it to the people of Paradise, al-Mawardi to the angels or believers, and Ibn Qayyim, followed by Ibn 'Ashur, sees it as the whole of creation. Several scholars, including Qatada, note that the Quran opens and closes with praise.
